q.intro.text: The Lincoln student council wants to know: do the two hundred forty seventh graders at Lincoln Middle get an hour of exercise most days? They asked sixty kids at the gym after school, and fifty-one said yes.

q.ask.text: What can the council say? Pick a statement, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Let's work it out, step by step. Press each step, and watch the map first, then the board.

e.step0.text: The population is all two hundred forty seventh graders at Lincoln Middle: everyone the question is about.

e.step1.text: The sample is the sixty kids at the gym. They are part of the population, and fifty-one of them said yes.

e.step2.text: Kids who go straight home after school were never asked. Kids at the gym are more likely to exercise, so fifty-one of sixty is likely too high for the whole grade.

e.step3.text: Not most of the two hundred forty: the data don't reach that far. The council can say fifty-one of the sixty kids at the gym get an hour most days.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why can't the council say most of Lincoln's seventh graders?

t.intro.text: Your turn. The Oak Hill librarian handed a reading survey to all two hundred students. A hundred forty forms came back, and a hundred ten said yes. Sixty were never returned. I'll do the first two steps.

t.clue.text: A clue: teachers noticed that students who don't like reading often left the form in their backpacks.

t.miss.text: For all two hundred students, is a hundred ten of a hundred forty likely too high, too low, or about right?

t.fill.text: Every way the sixty could have answered: if all sixty said yes, that's a hundred seventy of two hundred. If all said no, a hundred ten of two hundred.

t.state.text: Which statement can the librarian make about all two hundred students?

t.done.text: Even if all sixty said no, a hundred ten of two hundred is more than half. A claim may cover the whole group when it holds in every case.

p.intro.text: Maya writes in the Eastside paper: we asked two hundred students in the cafeteria line, and a hundred sixty like the new lunch menu. So most of the six hundred Eastside students like the new menu. Is Maya right, or does her claim go too far?

p.build.text: Prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The population is the whole group the question is about: all six hundred Eastside students.

p.c2.text: And every answer came from the lunch line. Students who bring lunch from home were never asked, and they may like the menu less.

p.c3.text: So the claim can only cover the group the data came from: a hundred sixty of the two hundred in line.

p.done.text: That's the argument. Who the question is about, who actually answered, and so how far the claim may reach.
